prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Let’s get this straight: Charles Graner is not America. America would never hold a knife to his wife’s throat, then say when she woke that he was considering killing her. And America’s wife in turn would never call her husband “my own Hannibal Lecter.” Am I right, or what? Charles Graner may be Hannibal Lecter, but he is not America. America is not that kind of husband. Nor would America email his adolescent children photos of himself torturing naked Iraqi prisoners and say “look what Daddy gets to do!” Am I right? America is not that kind of father. America would never torture naked Iraqi prisoners. Let’s be absolutely clear about all of this. And America’s ex-lover and co-defendant would never whisper to the sketch artist at America’s trial: “You forgot the horns.” Charles Graner may or may not have horns, but America is horn-free. America does not torture prisoners. America may render them, fully clothed, to Egypt or Syria, for further interrogation, or to men like Charles Graner, but America is not, ipso facto, Egypt or Syria, and Charles Graner is not now nor has he ever been America. And don’t talk to me about Guantanamo. Please! Let’s get this straight. You and I know who America is. We know what America does and doesn’t do, because we (not Charles Graner!) are America. Am I right? Is this all clear? Tell me—am I right, or what?

outputs.L3:
The text argues that Charles Graner’s abusive and violent behavior should not be treated as representative of America as a whole. It repeatedly insists that Graner, despite his role in the abuse of prisoners, is not the same thing as the nation he served. This distinction is central to the passage: the author presents Graner as an individual whose cruelty and brutality must be separated from the larger idea of America.

At the same time, the text contrasts Graner’s personal violence with an idealized image of America as morally innocent, decent, and fundamentally opposed to cruelty. America is presented, at least on the surface, as a nation that does not torture, does not abuse prisoners, and does not abandon its ethical principles. This idealized version of America is sharply opposed to the image of Graner as sadistic and corrupt.

However, the passage uses satire to undermine this comforting separation. While it appears to deny that America tortures prisoners, it simultaneously points to practices such as extraordinary rendition and the detention of prisoners at Guantanamo. These references suggest that the problem cannot be reduced to one man’s misconduct. By mentioning policies and institutions associated with abuse, the text exposes a gap between America’s self-image and its actions.

The repeated claim that “Charles Graner is not America” therefore becomes ironic. On one level, it attempts to isolate Graner’s wrongdoing and protect the nation from moral blame. On another level, the repetition draws attention to the difficulty of maintaining that separation. If abuse occurs within systems created, approved, or tolerated by the state, then national responsibility cannot be so easily dismissed.

Through irony and rhetorical questions, the passage challenges the reader to think more critically about American identity and accountability. It asks whether a country can preserve an image of innocence while benefiting from or ignoring violent practices carried out in its name. Ultimately, the text questions the desire to blame only individuals like Graner while avoiding a broader examination of the institutions and policies that made such abuses possible.
outputs.L4:
The text examines U.S. responsibility for torture and prisoner abuse through a sharply satirical voice. It repeatedly insists that “America” is not responsible for what happened at Abu Ghraib and that the blame belongs only to individuals such as Charles Graner. On the surface, these denials appear to defend the nation from association with torture. However, the repetition is so exaggerated and so obviously strained that it becomes ironic. Instead of persuading the reader that America is innocent, the text reveals how absurd and morally evasive such a defense is.

By separating “America” from Graner, Abu Ghraib, and other abuses, the text exposes a familiar pattern of official denial. Governments often respond to scandals by describing them as the actions of a few “bad apples,” rather than as the result of policies, institutions, and chains of command. The satire challenges this explanation. It suggests that torture and prisoner abuse cannot be understood only as the private cruelty of one soldier or one prison guard. Abu Ghraib was not an isolated moral failure; it existed within a broader context of war, detention, interrogation, secrecy, and dehumanization.

The text also connects Abu Ghraib to practices such as torture and rendition, showing that abuse was not confined to one prison or one group of perpetrators. Rendition, secret detention, and coercive interrogation depended on official decisions and legal justifications. By pretending that these acts were separate from “America,” public officials could avoid confronting the larger system that made them possible. The satire therefore attacks not only the abuse itself, but also the language used to excuse it.

The key point is that the attempt to divide the nation from its actions is morally dishonest. If abuses were carried out by American personnel, under American authority, in pursuit of American policy goals, then they cannot simply be dismissed as un-American exceptions. The repeated denials become a way of hiding responsibility rather than clarifying it. They allow the country to preserve an image of innocence while avoiding accountability for what was done in its name.

Ultimately, the text argues that disavowal is itself part of the problem. By insisting that torture does not represent “America,” officials and citizens can avoid asking harder questions about power, policy, and complicity. The satire forces readers to see that national innocence cannot be maintained merely by blaming a few individuals. The real issue is not whether Charles Graner personally behaved brutally, but whether a larger political and military system enabled, encouraged, excused, or concealed such brutality. In this way, the text uses irony to expose the gap between America’s self-image and the reality of its actions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical political monologue about Charles Graner and Abu Ghraib that repeatedly insists “Charles Graner is not America” while exposing the hypocrisy of U.S. torture policy.
counterfactuals.output:
Ladies and gentlemen, let us be absolutely clear: **Charles Graner is not America.**

No, no, no. Charles Graner—the former Army reservist convicted for his role in the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib—is *not* America. He is merely a tiny, disposable footnote in a much larger national scrapbook titled: *Things We Definitely Don’t Do, Except When We Do Them, But Only Because Freedom Is Complicated.*

**Charles Graner is not America.**  
America is bigger than one man posing next to naked detainees. America is an idea. A shining city on a hill. A Constitution in a glass case. A press conference with flags behind it. A legal memo with the word “torture” crossed out and replaced with “enhanced vibes.”

You see, when photographs from Abu Ghraib emerged, the official story was very simple: this was a few bad apples. A handful of rogue soldiers. A tragic deviation from American values.

And thank goodness, because if there’s one thing we know about bad apples, it’s that they spontaneously appear in perfectly healthy barrels, surrounded by memos, chain-of-command ambiguity, military intelligence pressure, contractor involvement, secret detention policies, and lawyers explaining that pain only counts if it reaches organ-failure levels.

But remember: **Charles Graner is not America.**

America would never torture. America merely asks stern questions in undisclosed locations. America does not violate human rights; it stress-tests them. America does not do cruelty; it conducts “interrogation innovation.” America does not disappear people; it renders them—like a nation-sized graphics card processing a war crime into a bureaucratic euphemism.

**Charles Graner is not America.**

He is not the policymakers who created the atmosphere.  
He is not the lawyers who tried to bend the Geneva Conventions into balloon animals.  
He is not the officials who said, “We don’t torture,” with the serene confidence of a man standing in front of a burning building and insisting it’s a barbecue.  
He is not the contractors, agencies, commanders, intelligence officers, committees, hearings, redactions, classified annexes, missing emails, or solemn statements about “lessons learned.”

No. Charles Graner is not America.

He is just the guy in the photo.

And that, my friends, is the genius of imperial accountability: put the whole machinery of policy behind a curtain, then point to the ugliest snapshot and say, “There! There is the problem. That man. That night shift. That prison wing. That grin.”

Because if Charles Graner is America, then America has to look in the mirror.

But if **Charles Graner is not America**, then America can look at the mirror, classify the mirror, redact the reflection, and issue a bipartisan statement thanking the mirror for its service.

We are told Abu Ghraib was an aberration. A stain. A mistake. But an aberration doesn’t come with footnotes. A mistake doesn’t have legal architecture. A stain doesn’t show up in multiple facilities under multiple programs while officials debate how much suffering can fit through a loophole.

Still, let us repeat the comforting phrase: **Charles Graner is not America.**

America is the country that condemns torture in other nations with a moral clarity so bright it can be seen from orbit. America publishes human rights reports. America lectures dictators. America imposes sanctions. America says, “A nation is judged by how it treats prisoners,” and then adds, very quietly, “depending on the classification of the prisoner, the location of the facility, the agency involved, and whether the photographer remembered to bring a camera.”

**Charles Graner is not America.**

America is not a hooded man standing on a box with wires attached to his hands. America is the official explanation that those wires weren’t actually connected to electricity, which apparently makes the whole thing less like torture and more like community theater with psychological trauma.

America is not the dog snarling at a detainee. America is the memo explaining the dog was part of an approved technique, unless it wasn’t, in which case a low-ranking soldier misunderstood the approved technique, which may not have been approved, though it was discussed, but not authorized, except verbally, maybe, by someone whose name is classified.

**Charles Graner is not America.**

America is due process—unless due process is inconvenient.  
America is the rule of law—unless the law is overseas.  
America is transparency—unless the documents are sensitive.  
America is accountability—unless accountability might climb the ladder.

So yes, punish Charles Graner. Punish the bad apple. Build the museum exhibit around the bad apple. Teach the children about the bad apple. Put the bad apple in the history book and say, “This is what happens when one apple goes wrong.”

But don’t ask who bought the barrel.  
Don’t ask who stored it in the dark.  
Don’t ask who removed the inspections.  
Don’t ask why the orchard kept producing the same fruit.

Because **Charles Graner is not America.**

He is what happens when America wants a defendant but not a diagnosis.

He is the convenient boundary line between “what we did” and “who we are.” He is the scapegoat with a court record, the face on the scandal, the human firewall protecting the servers of policy.

And yet, if Charles Graner is not America, then America must prove it—not by saying “never again” every time the photos surface, but by dismantling the legal, political, and moral machinery that made “again” possible in the first place.

Because a nation is not judged by whether it can find a few guilty hands at the bottom. It is judged by whether it has the courage to follow the chain upward.

So let us close with the official line, the soothing mantra, the lullaby of plausible deniability:

**Charles Graner is not America.**

But if America builds the policy, drafts the memos, ignores the warnings, hides the evidence, prosecutes downward, protects upward, rebrands torture, and then congratulates itself for accountability—

then maybe the problem was never that Charles Graner represented America.

Maybe the problem is that America worked very hard to make sure he wouldn’t have to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a biting, ironic essay in the style of early-2000s antiwar commentary, using rhetorical questions like “Am I right?” to argue that America disowns torturers while enabling torture through rendition and Guantanamo.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Torturers Are Not Us, Except When They Are**

One of the most comforting things about American democracy is that we are always shocked—shocked—by the things we authorized, funded, outsourced, renamed, redacted, and then solemnly deplored. There is no moral hygiene quite like discovering, after the fact, that torture has occurred somewhere in the machinery of empire and that, astonishingly, no one in polite society seems to have done it.

Because America, as every speechwriter knows, does not torture. America “detains.” America “questions.” America “renders.” America “processes” human beings through “facilities” in “theater,” where “enhanced techniques” may be applied by “personnel” acting under “guidance.” If the language is ugly enough, perhaps the deed will become invisible. Am I right?

And when it does become visible—when the hooded man appears in the photograph, when the cage at Guantanamo catches the light, when some poor soul dragged through an airport in shackles turns out to have a name, a family, and a spine no longer functioning properly—then comes the great national ritual of disowning. We look around the room and ask: Who invited the torturer?

Certainly not us.

Not the officials who wrote memos explaining that pain only really counts if it approaches organ failure. Not the legislators who preferred not to know too much, because knowledge is such a burden when one is busy being briefed. Not the commentators who spent years insisting that the Constitution is not a suicide pact, which apparently means it is a takeout menu. Not the voters who were told that somewhere, in a cell outside the reach of courts and cameras, a terrible man might know the location of a ticking bomb, and therefore all civilization depended on whether we could make him scream creatively enough.

No, the torturer is always someone else. A bad apple. A contractor. A foreign intelligence service with regrettable methods but excellent cooperation. A soldier “under stress.” A low-level interrogator. A distant ally. A legal ambiguity. A photograph without context. A footnote.

The genius of rendition was that it transformed torture into a travel arrangement. Why dirty your own hands when you can book the prisoner a flight? Why violate your principles domestically when there are runways in places where principles have less troublesome lawyers? A man is seized, hooded, diapered, shackled, flown across borders, delivered to a room where screams are less likely to be subpoenaed, and then—miracle of miracles—America remains pristine. We did not torture him. We merely transported him to people who did, while asking no questions in tones of grave strategic necessity.

Isn’t that the essence of innocence? To arrange the conditions under which a thing will happen and then stand at a diplomatic distance from the result? Am I right?

Guantanamo perfected the same moral magic trick in architectural form. It was designed as a nowhere place: close enough for American control, far enough for American law to arrive late and out of breath. A camp for “the worst of the worst,” we were told, a phrase that did a great deal of work before any evidence had to. Men could be held there not as prisoners of war, not as criminal defendants, not quite as human beings with ordinary claims on ordinary justice, but as a new category invented for the occasion: the sort of person to whom things may be done.

And what things? Stress positions, sleep deprivation, isolation, sensory assault, humiliation, the slow unmaking of a mind. But do not call it torture too quickly. That word is vulgar, and vulgarity is what separates us from our enemies. We prefer acronyms, authorizations, classified annexes. We prefer the clean prose of bureaucratic cruelty. We prefer to debate definitions while the body in question trembles.

The great trick was not merely to excuse torture, but to make opposition to it sound unserious. What would you do, then, offer terrorists a lawyer? Read them poetry? Serve tea? The question always came wrapped in adolescent certainty, as if the entire history of law, war, interrogation, intelligence, and human rights had been concocted by naïve graduate students who had never watched a season finale of a television thriller.

And the ticking bomb—always the ticking bomb. Somewhere in the fever dream of national security, there is always a ticking bomb. It ticks in op-eds. It ticks in Senate hearings. It ticks in the imagination of men who confuse toughness with wisdom and cruelty with adulthood. It ticks loudly enough to drown out the actual record: the false confessions, the ruined prosecutions, the radicalizing propaganda, the intelligence contaminated by agony, the allies disgusted, the enemies delighted, the victims who were innocent, the guilty who became harder to try because we chose to become what we claimed to oppose.

But never mind all that. There is a bomb, hypothetical and eternal, and because it might be ticking, the law must be made to crawl.

Then, after the damage is done, the same chorus returns to assure us that America is bigger than its mistakes. Bigger, certainly. Bigger than the cells, bigger than the black sites, bigger than the men disappeared into cooperating dictatorships, bigger than the photographs, bigger than the memos, bigger than the courts that were told to wait, bigger than the graves. America is always large enough to absorb responsibility without quite experiencing accountability.

We regret. We review. We move forward. We do not look backward, because looking backward is divisive, and nothing divides a country like asking who ordered the crimes.

So the torturers are disowned, but the system that required them remains. The hand is condemned; the glove is preserved. The interrogator is an embarrassment; the policy is a difficult choice. The photograph is an outrage; the architecture is national security. We deplore the stain while keeping the ink.

This is the empire’s moral laundering service: send violence abroad, classify the receipt, rename the act, prosecute the expendable, promote the respectable, and deliver a speech about values. Am I right?

The irony is not that America failed to live up to its ideals. Nations often fail. The deeper disgrace is that the ideals were kept on display while the exceptions multiplied in secret. The flag stayed clean because the dirty work was done just outside the frame. The anthem played while the plane took off. The Constitution slept while the memo explained.

And when history finally asks what happened, we will say what powerful countries always say: mistakes were made, lessons were learned, safeguards were strengthened. Passive voice, active impunity.

No one tortured.

No one authorized torture.

No one enabled torture.

No one built the rooms, signed the cables, leased the aircraft, drafted the definitions, ignored the warnings, or applauded the toughness.

It simply happened, somehow, in the shadows cast by a nation that insisted it was standing in the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short piece of dark political satire about the Abu Ghraib scandal, mentioning Charles Graner, Hannibal Lecter, naked Iraqi prisoners, Egypt, Syria, and Guantanamo, with a sarcastic patriotic refrain.
counterfactuals.output:
At Abu Ghraib, the empire discovered a new kind of flag-waving: not cloth in the wind, but paperwork in triplicate, denials in formation, and naked Iraqi prisoners arranged like footnotes nobody in Washington wanted to read.

Charles Graner smiled for history’s ugliest yearbook photo, while the brass explained that morality had been subcontracted, misplaced, or perhaps renditioned through Egypt, Syria, and Guantanamo for “enhanced” clarification.

Somewhere, Hannibal Lecter might have raised an eyebrow and said, “Even I prefer a little elegance with my depravity.”

But never mind. The anthem swells, the cameras blink, the memos vanish into patriotic fog:

**God bless the chain of command,  
from sea to shining alibi.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a sarcastic rant that personifies America as morally innocent and contrasts it with Charles Graner’s abuses, gradually revealing that the denial is hypocritical and absurd.
counterfactuals.output:
Oh, America? America would *never*.

America is a bright-eyed choirboy in a pressed white shirt, standing in the morning sun with one hand over its heart and the other hand discreetly behind its back, because whatever is in that hand is probably classified and anyway you’re being very negative. America believes in freedom, in dignity, in the sacred worth of the individual—especially when the individual is conveniently abstract, preferably in a speech, ideally backlit by flags.

Charles Graner? Well, that was different. That was ugly. That was the work of a bad man in a bad place doing bad things, and thank goodness America was nowhere nearby, except for the uniforms, the prison, the chain of command, the war, the memos, the euphemisms, the policy climate, the cameras, the grinning, the silence, and the flag stitched neatly on the shoulder.

But America itself? Innocent. Pure as a civics textbook. America did not stack naked detainees into pyramids. America did not put people on leashes. America did not smile over human humiliation as if cruelty were a hunting trophy. No, no—those were merely the actions of individuals, and individuals are famously unrelated to institutions, unless they win medals or invent useful technology, in which case they are proof of national greatness.

America was shocked—*shocked*—to discover abuse occurring in a prison it controlled during a war it launched under doctrines it refined with language so sterile it could make a broken body sound like a paperwork issue. “Enhanced.” “Stress position.” “Softening up.” Such delicate phrases. You could embroider them on a pillow and give it to a think tank.

And poor America, always so misunderstood. It only wanted to liberate. It only wanted to bring democracy. If a few people were stripped, terrorized, degraded, and photographed under fluorescent lights, surely that was not America’s soul showing through a crack in the plaster. Surely that was an accident, a lapse, a glitch in the freedom machine. The machine itself remains noble. Please do not look at the gears.

Because Charles Graner is useful. He is a container. Put the horror in him, seal the lid, label it “bad apple,” and suddenly the barrel is innocent. The orchard is innocent. The farmer is innocent. The weather is innocent. The country that built the barrel, filled it, shipped it overseas, and then expressed deep disappointment when it leaked rot all over the floor—spotless.

America wept when it saw the photos, or at least it made the correct facial expression. America condemned the cruelty in the strongest possible terms, which is the traditional ritual by which power washes its hands without getting them wet. It promised investigations. It promised accountability. It promised that this was not who “we” are, because “we” are apparently a nation that can do things repeatedly while remaining metaphysically incapable of being the kind of nation that does them.

That’s the beauty of innocence on this scale: it is indestructible. If America feeds the hungry, that is America. If America bombs a wedding, that is a tragic error. If America builds a school, that is America. If America builds a prison where men are disappeared into screams and paperwork, that is a regrettable deviation from values. Values, you understand, are what America has when no one is checking the basement.

So yes, blame Graner. Blame his cruelty, his arrogance, his obscene little theater of domination. He earned that blame. But let’s not pretend the stage assembled itself. Let’s not pretend the script floated down from nowhere. Let’s not pretend the audience of commanders, contractors, lawyers, politicians, and citizens were all just helplessly surprised to find that a war sold as moral necessity had developed a moral smell.

America, dear innocent America, stands there blinking under the spotlight, saying, “I don’t know how this could have happened,” while wearing the costume, holding the keys, cashing the checks, saluting the mission, and insisting the stain on its sleeve is somebody else’s shadow.

And maybe that is the most American miracle of all: to be present everywhere, responsible nowhere, forever betrayed by the consequences of one’s own power.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a punchy satirical column opening with “Let’s get this straight: Charles Graner is not America,” repeating the phrase “America would never,” and ending with “Tell me—am I right, or what?”
counterfactuals.output:
Let’s get this straight: Charles Graner is not America. America would never confuse cruelty with policy, or paperwork with conscience. America would never build a cathedral to accountability and then misplace the key whenever the basement starts screaming. America would never look at a photograph, squint hard enough to blur the uniforms, and declare the problem solved because one bad apple has been sternly identified, labeled, and rolled ceremoniously away from the barrel.

No, America would never. America would never outsource its nightmares, redact its memories, or promote the soothing national bedtime story that every scandal begins and ends with the one guy careless enough to get caught smiling. We are, after all, a nation of principles—especially when those principles can be printed on a podium backdrop, laminated for hearings, and filed under “lessons learned” before lunch.

Tell me—am I right, or what?
